name: Colored / circle contact lenses
lead: Colored contact lenses, also called cosmetic, decorative or fashion lenses, change the apparent colour of the eye. Circle lenses, also called big-eye lenses, are a type of cosmetic lens that adds a coloured or dark ring to enlarge the apparent size of the iris. [1]

In the United States the Food and Drug Administration regulates decorative lenses as medical devices, requires a prescription for them, and warns that lenses obtained without a proper fitting can cause corneal abrasion, allergic reactions, reduced vision and infections that may lead to blindness. [2]

In looksmaxxing communities, coloured lenses are discussed as a way to lighten or contrast the eye colour, especially for people with dark brown eyes, and users debate shades, wear time and whether the result looks natural. No controlled study of their effect on perceived attractiveness was found. [3][4]

paras: Cosmetic lenses can be plano (no vision correction) or made with a prescription. They may tint the iris colour, print an opaque pattern, or add a darker or larger rim in the case of circle lenses, which are intended to make the eyes appear bigger. [1] A report published in BMC Medical Imaging notes that circle lenses usually contain iron oxide and other metals in their pigment, which is why they may be a hazard during magnetic resonance imaging. [1]

The FDA states that decorative contact lenses are medical devices that must be prescribed by a doctor, with the prescription listing the brand, lens measurements and expiry date. It advises buying only from sellers that require a prescription and sell FDA-cleared lenses, and it names street vendors, beauty-supply and novelty shops and unknown online sellers as sources of potentially contaminated or counterfeit products. [2]

The agency lists corneal abrasion, allergic reaction, decreased vision and infection as risks of lenses worn without a proper fit or prescription, and advises seeking an eye doctor immediately for redness, persistent eye pain or reduced vision. It also advises against sharing lenses. [2]
Case reporting adds a specific imaging concern: a published case described the incidental discovery of circle lenses on an MRI scan, with the authors noting the metal content of the pigment. [1]
No clinical trials of coloured or circle lenses as an appearance intervention were found. The published literature on them consists mainly of case reports such as the MRI report. [1]

Forum threads ask which colours suit a particular complexion and hair colour, and how to get a green or hazel result over dark brown eyes while keeping a natural look. One poster lists requirements of light green or hazel colour, a natural appearance, a pupil opening that does not obscure vision, and longer wear times. [3] Another asks whether lenses can be ordered online without knowing eye measurements. [4] Thread titles include claims that lenses are a large 'ascension', that wearing them is the 'ultimate cope', and personal accounts of what lenses did for the poster. [5][6][7]

card.summary: Tinted or enlarging contact lenses that change eye colour; FDA treats them as prescription medical devices with infection risks.
card.aka: Circle lenses, big-eye lenses, cosmetic contacts
card.note: FDA warns that unfitted or non-prescribed lenses can cause infection and vision loss.

quick.overview:
Coloured and circle lenses are cosmetic contacts that change the look of the iris, either by tinting it or by adding a ring that makes the eye appear larger. In forums they are mostly used to lighten dark eyes.

No studies were found that measure whether they raise perceived attractiveness, so the appearance benefit rests on user reports.
quick.mechanism: A printed pigment layer on the lens covers or modifies the iris colour, and circle lenses add a darker or larger outer rim to enlarge the visible iris.
quick.risks: The FDA classes decorative lenses as medical devices needing a prescription and lists corneal abrasion, allergy, reduced vision and infection that can lead to blindness. A case report notes that some circle lenses contain metals that can matter during MRI.
